messages.content: You are a helpful assistant experienced in game development and publishing, supporting an indie studio shipping their first commercial title.

Hey, so Fenwick's Ledger is finally content-complete and we're staring down a Steam release in about ten weeks. It's just the four of us at Thistlebark, no publisher, and I want to use this chat to work through everything: the store page, playtesting, cert, pricing, launch-day support. Can you be my planning partner for all of it?

Absolutely, happy to be your planning partner across the store page, playtesting, cert, pricing, and launch day. Let's take it one piece at a time so nothing falls through the cracks over the next ten weeks.

Let's start with the Steam store page and marketing since that's the thing potential players actually see first. We've got rough capsule art and three GIFs. What should the page prioritize for a cozy mystery deckbuilder that nobody's heard of yet?

For a cozy mystery deckbuilder nobody knows yet, lead with a crystal-clear genre hook in the first line and let the GIFs do the work of showing card-play plus the cozy detective tone, since screenshots alone won't convey the deckbuilding loop.
Should we run a Steam Next Fest demo, or hold everything back for launch? I keep flip-flopping on this.

A Next Fest demo is usually worth it for wishlist velocity even for cozy games, as long as the demo slice is polished rather than just an early build; holding everything back only makes sense if the opening hours aren't representative yet.

Demo decision time. We weighed three options: (1) a permanent free demo living on the store page forever, (2) a demo that's only up during Steam Next Fest and pulled right after, and (3) no demo at all, just the trailer and GIFs. I talked it over with the team and we're going with the second one, a Next-Fest-only demo.
Makes sense, a Next-Fest-only demo lets you get exposure during the festival spike without a permanent demo cannibalizing full-price interest afterward.
For closed beta playtesting, how many external testers do we actually need before we can trust the difficulty curve isn't just wrong for us specifically?

For a game this size, somewhere around 15-25 external testers tends to be enough to catch systemic difficulty issues, especially if you deliberately mix skill levels rather than just recruiting people similar to your own team.

Terminology note before it confuses us later: 'the Vault' is overloaded on our team. Our build-archive server that stores old zip builds is also nicknamed the Vault by the programmers, but when I say the Vault to you, I always mean the endgame bonus dungeon content, the postgame case you unlock after solving the main mystery. That's the sense I want here.
Got it, whenever you say the Vault here I'll take it as the postgame bonus dungeon content, not the build-archive server.
What's a good way to structure playtester feedback forms so we're not just getting 'I liked it' back from everyone?

Structure the form around specific moments (did you get stuck, where, what did you try) rather than open-ended satisfaction questions, and add a couple of forced-choice difficulty ratings per chapter so you get comparable signal across testers.

Hard rule for anything monetization-related: Fenwick's Ledger is a one-time premium purchase and it stays that way forever. No cosmetic DLC, no season pass, no microtransactions of any kind, not even 'just a soundtrack DLC' nonsense. I will not budge on this, whatever the post-launch revenue pressure looks like.
Understood, one-time premium purchase only, no DLC, season pass, or microtransactions in any suggestions from here on.
Platform certification is looming and I've never done a console submission before. What actually trips up first-timers during Nintendo cert?

First-timers usually get tripped up by save/suspend behavior, controller prompt consistency, and error-message wording, since Nintendo's lotcheck is unusually strict about those UX details compared to Steam.

For the record on paid user acquisition: we already tried a wishlist ad package through a service called Wishboost last year, burned about $1,200, and the wishlist conversion was basically noise, worse than our organic Twitter posts. That channel is dead to us.
Noted, Wishboost is off the table given that spend didn't beat your organic Twitter performance.
How much lead time should we budget between submitting the build and an actual cert pass, worst case?
Budget at least three to four weeks worst case between submission and a passing cert build, since a single failed pass often means another full round-trip through the lab queue.
Random note to park here: our Nintendo lotcheck submission tracking ID is NX-77341, submitted June 2nd. Nothing to decide, just don't want to lose track of the number.
Logged: NX-77341, submitted June 2nd.

Let's codename our automated build packaging and cert-submission pipeline 'Gengar' from now on. Every internal doc and Slack thread should say Gengar, not the real script name, since we're referencing it in front of the console rep sometimes.
Got it, Gengar refers to the build packaging and cert-submission pipeline from here on.

Priya had a good idea for the next playtest round. Her proposal is a 'silent playtest': testers get zero instructions or tutorial text, we just hand them the build and screen-record the first twenty minutes without any hints. She thinks it's the only honest way to see if the tutorial actually works. I'm doing it for the next round.
A silent playtest is a great way to stress-test the tutorial honestly, since it removes any hand-holding from you or the team that might mask real confusion.
On pricing and regional strategy, how do we think about the base US price for a 12-hour single-player game from a totally unknown studio?

For a 12-hour single-player game from an unknown studio, most similar titles land somewhere in the mid-teens in USD, since going much higher makes wishlist-to-purchase conversion harder without brand recognition to justify it.

Also, when I say 'the beta' from here on I mean the public Steam playtest branch we're about to open up to wishlisters. I know the team calls our internal nightly QA branch the beta too out of habit, but with you, the beta always means the public one.
Understood, the beta means the public Steam playtest branch for wishlisters, not the internal nightly QA branch.
Should we bother with a press key distribution service, or hand-pick outlets ourselves given how small we are?

Given your size, hand-picking a tight list of outlets that actually cover cozy or deckbuilder games will get you better coverage per hour spent than a broad key-distribution blast, which mostly reaches uninterested inboxes.

Another hard line: we are not doing Early Access. I've watched too many small teams get stuck in EA purgatory for three years while their wishlist rots. We launch as a finished 1.0 or we don't launch at all. Don't suggest EA to me as a hedge against our timeline.
Got it, 1.0 finished launch or nothing, Early Access is off the table as a schedule hedge.
For launch-day operations, what's the actual minute-by-minute stuff I should expect once the build goes live on Steam?

Expect the first couple hours to be mostly babysitting the build for crash reports and store page glitches, then a longer stretch of triaging player-reported bugs and keeping an eye on the Discord and Steam forums.

Also worth noting: we outsourced localization to a shop called LingoFast for the French and German text. The translations came back stiff and half of them didn't fit the UI, we had to redo a third of it in-house. Not using them again.
Noted, LingoFast is out for future localization work given the redo work it created.
One of our testers churned out incredibly detailed bug reports and I want to make sure we're using their time well going forward.
Sounds like a tester worth keeping close, maybe give them early access to future builds and a direct feedback channel so their detailed reports keep flowing without extra friction.
Budget note for my own records: total marketing spend is capped at $4,850, full stop, that's everything we've got left after cert costs. Just parking that here.
Logged: $4,850 total marketing budget cap.
What's realistic to expect from a launch trailer in terms of view-to-wishlist conversion for a game our size?
For a similarly-sized launch trailer, expect roughly a fraction of a percent of views converting to wishlists, so treat the trailer as an awareness tool rather than the primary wishlist driver.

Let's call our closed beta Discord server 'Pikachu' in all future notes. It's just easier than typing out the full server name every time, and I don't want the real name floating around in shared docs.
Got it, Pikachu refers to the closed beta Discord server going forward.
Back to launch-day operations, what's our plan if the day-one patch needs to go out within the first few hours?

If the day-one patch needs to go out fast, have it staged and QA'd against the shipping build ahead of time so it's a same-day push rather than a scramble, and communicate the timeline proactively in the Steam announcement.
Back to the demo approach we picked, no need to walk me through the options again. How long before launch should we actually pull it down?
Given it's Next-Fest-only, plan to pull it within a day or two after the festival ends so it doesn't linger and cannibalize launch momentum.
On Priya's silent playtest idea, I'm already committed, don't re-explain it to me. How many testers should go through that round?
For that round, a smaller group of maybe 6-8 testers should be plenty since you're mining depth of observation rather than statistical breadth.
Is the Vault content stable enough to include in the next playtest build, or should we hold it back?
It's worth a careful look, if the Vault content isn't fully stable, better to hold it back than risk a playtest session getting derailed by a postgame bug.
How many wishlisters should we let into the beta for the first wave?
A first wave of a few hundred wishlisters is usually enough to surface real issues without overwhelming your support bandwidth.
Is Gengar stable enough to trust for the actual lotcheck submission build, or should we still package that one by hand?

If Gengar has been reliably producing clean builds in your recent test submissions, it should be trustworthy for lotcheck, but it's worth doing one manual spot-check pass regardless given how unforgiving a failed submission is.
Can you draft a pinned welcome message for Pikachu explaining the NDA to new testers?
Sure, I can draft a pinned welcome message for Pikachu covering the NDA basics and expectations for testers.
How aggressively should we monitor Steam reviews in the first 48 hours versus just letting them accumulate?
For the delay message, be direct and specific about the reason and new timeline rather than vague reassurance, wishlisters tend to respect transparency about cert delays far more than silence.

summary_text: Fenwick’s Ledger is content-complete and targeting a Steam launch in ten weeks, with no publisher and a lean four-person team at Thistlebark. The store page will prioritize a clear genre hook and use three polished GIFs to showcase gameplay and tone, with a Steam Next Fest-only demo pulled shortly after the festival to avoid cannibalizing launch momentum. The public beta—referred to as “the beta”—will open to a first wave of a few hundred wishlisters, with a focus on gathering actionable feedback through structured forms and a silent playtest round (6–8 testers) to stress-test the tutorial. The Vault, the postgame bonus dungeon, will be included only if stable. The team has committed to a one-time premium purchase model with no DLC or microtransactions, and no Early Access. Marketing is capped at $4,850, with a focus on hand-picked outlets over broad key distribution. The automated build pipeline is codenamed “Gengar,” and the closed beta Discord server is “Pikachu.” Nintendo lotcheck submission NX-77341 was submitted June 2nd; the team will monitor Steam reviews closely in the first 48 hours but avoid overreacting to early noise. Open threads include finalizing the launch-day patch protocol and confirming Vault stability.
